4.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is a screw, name its parts"
- "A screw is a device that **converts rotation into linear motion**; the head stops it, the thread pulls, the preload compresses."
- "Parts: **head** with its recess, **shank**, **run-out**, **thread**, **tip**; measures: **core diameter**, **outer diameter**, **thread depth**, **pitch** and **lead**."

### Parts, one line each
| Part | What it is | Exam point |
|---|---|---|
| **Head** | wider than the thread → acts as a stop | holds the recess for the screwdriver (AO) |
| **Recess** | hexagonal or star socket | hex → torque spread over 6 points (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| **Underside of head** | spherical (hemispherical) | stays congruous when the screw is tilted in a plate hole (AO) |
| **Shank** | smooth part between head and thread | almost absent in cortex screws; present in cancellous and lag-by-design screws (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| **Run-out** | junction of shank and thread | **weakest point** → breaks here (Nagah) |
| **Thread** | helical inclined plane around the core | gives purchase in bone (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| **Tip** | blunt, self-tapping or self-drilling | decides whether you tap (AO) |

- Parts of a cortex screw: head, run-out, thread, tip (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Cortical and cancellous screws with labelled parts (Nagah)

### How it works
- Rotation → thread slides on the bone thread → screw advances → head meets cortex → **preload** (AO)
- Preload compresses the fracture · **friction** between fracture surfaces and under the head resists shear (AO)
- Torque on a 4.5 mm cortex screw → **50%** head friction · **40%** axial force · **10%** thread friction (AO)

### The head and its recess
- Recess types → slotted · cruciate · Phillips · **hexagonal (Allen)** · **Torx (Stardrive)** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **Hexagonal** = most used · strips with excess torque or a worn screwdriver → 4.7 (AO)
- Stardrive → better torque transmission, less stripping → used on most current plates and screws (Prof Abdel Karim)

- 3.5 cortex and 4.0 cancellous → head **6 mm**, socket 2.5 mm (Handbook)
- 4.5 cortex and 6.5 cancellous → head **8 mm**, socket 3.5 mm (Handbook)

- Head recess types (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Hexagonal and Stardrive recesses, photos (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Diameters and thread depth
- **Core (root, inner) diameter** → narrowest → sets the **pilot drill** and the bending strength (AO)
- **Outer (thread, nominal) diameter** → names the screw ("4.5", "3.5") → sets the **gliding drill** and the **tap** (AO)
- **Thread depth = (outer − core) / 2** → deeper thread → more pull-out strength (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Example → 3.5 cortex: outer 3.5, core 2.5 → depth 0.5 mm (Handbook)

| Property | Depends on | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Bending strength | **core diameter³** → double the core = 8× | Prof Abdel Karim |
| Tensile strength | core (root) diameter² | Prof Abdel Karim · Miller |
| Pull-out strength | **outer diameter**, length in bone, bone density | Rockwood |
| Stiffness | radius⁴ → a 6 mm screw ≈5× stiffer than a 3 mm | Rockwood |

- **Max pull-out** → large outer diameter · small root diameter · **fine pitch** (Miller)
- Core up **30%** → bending resistance ≈**3×**, little loss of pull-out (AO)

- Core, outer diameter and thread depth (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Pitch and lead
- **Pitch** = distance between adjacent threads · **lead** = advance per 360° turn (Miller)
- Single-start (all standard screws) → **pitch = lead** · multi-start → **lead = pitch × starts** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **Fine pitch** → cortex and locking screws · **coarse pitch** → cancellous screws (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Pitch of cortex screws → 3.5 = **1.25 mm** (Nagah) · 4.5 = **1.75 mm** (AO)
- Pitch of cancellous screws → 4.0 = 1.75 mm · 6.5 = **2.75 mm** (Nagah)

- Pitch and lead: one start versus two starts (Prof Abdel Karim)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Core → pilot drill, bending · outer → gliding drill, tap, pull-out · pitch = lead if single start**

### Run-out, thread profile, tip
- Run-out = abrupt change of diameter → **stress riser** → torsional break with a spiral surface (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Old run-out = outer diameter → bone burst in the pilot hole · modern **undercut (trimmed)** run-out (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **V-thread** → slanted both sides, compression + shear · **buttress (AO) thread** → flat trailing edge facing the head, mainly compression (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Same pull-out for both at equal outer diameter · buttress → less loosening long term (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Run-out: oversized versus trimmed (undercut) (Prof Abdel Karim)
- V-thread versus buttress thread profiles (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Design parameters of a bone screw (Campbell)

| Tip | Looks like | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Blunt (rounded, conical)** | smooth end | only after **tapping**; best pull-out (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| **Self-tapping** | **cutting flutes** at the tip | cuts its thread, flutes carry chips (AO) |
| **Self-drilling** | drill-like point | drills + taps; locking screws in MIPO (minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis) (Handbook) |
| **Corkscrew (spiral)** | thread to the end | pushes cancellous bone aside, cannulated screws (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| **Trocar** | sharp pointed | malleolar screw (Nagah) |

- Standard, self-tapping and self-drilling tips (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Working length
- **Working length** = thread anchored in bone → long → low bone–screw stress (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Short → thin osteoporotic cortex, monocortical screw · long → thick cortex, bicortical (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Short versus long working length, interface stress (Prof Abdel Karim)

4.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which screw is this?"
- "Threaded all along, fine shallow thread, no shank → **cortex screw**; deep coarse thread, often a smooth shank → **cancellous screw**."
- "Threads on the head → **locking head screw**; hollow → **cannulated**; no head, two pitches → **headless (Herbert)**."

| Screw | Look for | Thread | Main use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cortex** | fully threaded, no shank | fine pitch, shallow | diaphysis, plate screw, lag by technique (AO) |
| **Cancellous** | fully or partially threaded, smooth shank | coarse pitch, deep | metaphysis, epiphysis (AO) |
| **Malleolar** | partial thread, **trocar tip** | cancellous-type | medial malleolus (Nagah) |
| **Locking head** | **threaded conical head** | fine, shallow, large core | locking plates (AO) |
| **Cannulated** | hole along the axis, guide wire | cancellous-type | femoral neck → ch 6, scaphoid (Campbell) |
| **Headless (Herbert, Acutrak)** | no head, two pitches | differential | scaphoid, articular fragments (Campbell) |

- Cortex and cancellous screws, photo (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Cortex, cancellous and locking head screws a–f (AO)

### Cortex vs cancellous
| | Cortex screw | Cancellous screw |
|---|---|---|
| Bone | dense, thin | porous, large volume (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| Pitch, thread | small pitch, small depth | larger pitch, **deeper** thread, larger outer diameter (AO) |
| Core | large → bending, fatigue strength | smaller → weaker in bending (Handbook) |
| Threading | fully threaded | fully or partially threaded (Handbook) |
| Tapping | tap or self-tapping | thread-forming → tap the near cortex only, if at all (Prof Abdel Karim) |

- Cancellous **thread length** → 16 mm or 32 mm, or fully threaded (Prof Abdel Karim) · "16/32" = thread, not screw length (Nagah)
- Partially threaded cancellous → **lag screw** · fully threaded → below (Nagah)

- 6.5 mm cancellous screws, three thread lengths (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Cortical and cancellous screws, photo (Campbell)

### Malleolar screw — card
- Recognise it → partially threaded, **trocar (trephine) tip**, self-tapping (Handbook) · **4.5 mm** (Campbell)
- Used for the medial malleolus and ligament avulsions (Campbell)

- Malleolar screw, trocar tip, photo (Nagah)

PITFALL — malleolar screw "4 mm"?
- Nagah → 4 mm, no tap
- Campbell → **4.5 mm**, self-tapping trephine tip
- Say → "**4.5 mm malleolar screw, trocar tip, no tap needed**"

### Sets and sizes
- **Mini** (1.5, 2.0 mm) · **small** (3.5, 4.0 mm) · **large** (4.5, 6.5 mm) (Nagah)
- Common outer diameters → 1.5, 2, 2.4, 2.7, 3.5, 4.5, 6.5, 7.3 mm (Rockwood)

| Screw | Outer | Core | Pilot drill | Gliding drill | Tap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.7 cortex | 2.7 | — | **2.0** | 2.7 | 2.7 (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| 3.5 cortex | 3.5 | 2.5 | **2.5** | 3.5 | 3.5 (Prof Abdel Karim) |
| 4.5 cortex | 4.5 | ≈3 | **3.2** | 4.5 | 4.5 (Campbell) |
| 4.0 cancellous | 4.0 | — | 2.5 | — | 3.5 (Campbell) |
| 6.5 cancellous | 6.5 | as 4.5 | **3.2** | shank 4.5 | **6.5** (Campbell) |

- Mini, small and large fragment sets (Prof Abdel Karim)
- 4.5 cortex screw: core and outer diameters (Prof Abdel Karim)
- 3.5 cancellous lag screw: core, shank, outer diameters (Prof Abdel Karim)

PITFALL — examiner's drill trap
- 4.5 screw → pilot **3.2**, not 3.5 · 3.5 screw → pilot **2.5**, not 2.7 · 2.7 screw → pilot 2.0 (Prof Abdel Karim)
- 6.5 cancellous → **same drill as the 4.5**, only the tap differs (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Say → "**pilot = core, gliding = outer, tap = outer**"

PITFALL — core of the 4.5 cortex screw
- AO → **3.0 mm** · Prof Abdel Karim → 3.1 mm · Rockwood and Handbook → 3.2 mm
- All agree on the **3.2 mm drill**, slightly bigger than the core
- Say → "**core about 3 mm, drill 3.2**"

### Self-tapping vs non-self-tapping
| | Non-self-tapping (blunt) | Self-tapping (fluted) |
|---|---|---|
| Steps | drill → **tap** → screw | drill → screw |
| Pull-out | higher, full thread contact (Prof Abdel Karim) | flutes reduce contact → less pull-out (AO) |
| Length | just past the far cortex | **2 mm longer**, flutes must clear the cortex (AO) |
| Problem | extra step | misdirection, hard removal from bony ingrowth (AO) |

- Self-tapping still needs a **tap in hard young cortex**, esp. 3.5 and 2.7 → heads break (AO)
- **Self-drilling** → length cannot be measured → most are cannulated, put over a guide wire (AO)
- Self-drilling may **fail to grip** → the drill tip cannot advance as fast as the thread pitch demands (AO)

### When fully threaded?
- **Cortex screws** → always fully threaded → plate screw, position screw, lag by technique (Handbook)
- Fully threaded cancellous → plate screw in metaphyseal bone (Nagah)
- Fully threaded lag screw needs a **gliding hole** → else the near thread blocks gliding (Rockwood)

### Locking head screw — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "locking head screw"
- "**Threaded conical head** that locks into a threaded plate hole → **angular stable** construct, plate not pressed on bone."
- "**Internal fixator** principle; stability from the screw–plate couple, not friction; **cannot be a lag screw**."

- Thread → **larger core**, shallow blunt thread, fine pitch → more strength, larger bone interface (AO)
- Load passes through the plate → **bending moment at the head–shaft junction** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Last turns **by hand with a torque-limiting screwdriver** → no jamming (AO)
- **Combination hole** → locking or conventional screw · titanium locking screws → **no failure in >2,000** monitored (AO)

- Locking head screw and threaded plate hole (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Locking head screw in a locking plate (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Conventional versus locked screw load transfer (Prof Abdel Karim)

| | Conventional plate screw | Locking head screw |
|---|---|---|
| Stability from | **friction** plate ↔ bone | **mechanical couple** screw ↔ plate |
| Plate–bone contact | yes, compressed | no |
| Principle | compression | internal fixator |
| Load | preload + friction | bending of the screw (Prof Abdel Karim) |

- **Variable-angle locking** → **15° each way** (30° cone) through an angle guide (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Variable-angle head → spherical · fixed-angle head → conical → **never mix them** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **NCB polyaxial** → plain head locked by a **cap** screwed into the plate hole (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Variable-angle locking screw, 30° cone (Prof Abdel Karim)

4.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "functions of screws"
- "**Plate screw**, **lag screw**, **position screw**, **locking head screw**, **interlocking screw**, **anchor screw**, **push–pull**, **reduction** and **Poller screw**."
- "Lag is a **function**, not a design: any screw that compresses across the fracture by gliding near and gripping far."

| Function | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Plate screw** | preload + friction, plate pressed on bone | forearm LC-DCP (limited-contact dynamic compression plate) (AO) |
| **Lag screw** | glide hole → interfragmentary compression | butterfly fragment, medial malleolus (AO) |
| **Position screw** | thread hole only, **no glide hole** → no compression | **syndesmotic screw**, distal humerus with a defect (AO) |
| **Locking head screw** | head locks in plate → angular stability | LCP (locking compression plate) in osteoporosis (AO) |
| **Interlocking screw** | couples nail to bone → length, alignment, rotation | locked tibial or femoral nail (AO) |
| **Anchor screw** | holds a wire loop or strong suture | tension band, proximal humerus (AO) |
| **Push–pull screw** | temporary point for distraction or compression | articulated tension device (AO) |
| **Reduction screw** | pulls a fragment to the plate, later exchanged | MIPO onto an LCP (AO) |
| **Poller screw** | fulcrum redirecting a nail | proximal tibial nailing (AO) |

- Plate screw pressing the plate on bone (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Anchor screw for a tension band, X-ray (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Push–pull screw with articulated tension device (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Articulated tension device → hook at the **acute angle** → fracture closes · obtuse angle → shear, overlap (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Pointers → interference screw ch 9 · pedicle screw ch 13 · plate functions ch 5 · femoral neck screws ch 6

EXAM PEARL — screws in a plate (details → ch 5)
- Max screw tilt in a **DCP** hole → **25° along** the plate, **7° across** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **Plate span ratio** 2–3× fracture length · **screw density** <0.5 (Prof Abdel Karim; AO)

4.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "lag screw"
- "Lag is a **technique**: thread grips the **far** fragment only, the near fragment glides → tightening pulls the fragments together = **interfragmentary compression**."
- "By technique → fully threaded screw, **gliding hole** = outer diameter, **pilot hole** = core."
- "By design → **partially threaded** screw with every thread beyond the fracture."

### Why a gliding hole?
- No gliding hole → thread holds both cortices → head seats, **gap stays or opens** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Undersized gliding hole (3.2 drill for a 3.5 screw) → no compression, near cortex stressed (Prof Abdel Karim)
- 4.5 mm screws tightened by experts → **2,000–3,000 N** of axial compression (AO)
- Compression fades over months but outlasts osteon bridging → **primary bone healing** (AO)

- Screw without a gliding hole (Prof Abdel Karim)

PITFALL — "2,500–3,000 N" and "2.5 N"
- Nagah oral notes → 2,500–3,000 N · Nagah implant notes → "2.5 N" (a slip)
- AO and Rockwood → **2,000–3,000 N**
- Say → "**a 4.5 lag screw gives about 2,000–3,000 N**"

### Lag by technique — steps (4.5 cortex screw)
1) **Reduce** and hold → Weber (pointed reduction) clamp (Prof Abdel Karim)
2) **Gliding hole** in the near cortex → **4.5 drill**, at 90° to the fracture (AO)
3) **Drill sleeve** in the gliding hole → **pilot hole** in the far cortex, **3.2 drill** (AO)
4) **Countersink** the near cortex (AO)
5) **Depth gauge** → screw length (Campbell)
6) **Tap 4.5** → thread in the far cortex only (Campbell)
7) **Screw** → pushed through the gliding hole, then turned → compression (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Lag screw perpendicular, or halfway, to the fracture (AO)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you insert a screw?"
- "**Drill** the pilot hole (core size) through a **drill sleeve**, **countersink** if no plate, **measure** with the depth gauge, **tap** (outer size), insert the **screw**."
- "Sharp bit, irrigation, sleeve → no heat necrosis; tap through a tap sleeve; final turns by hand."

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Drill bit → drill sleeve → countersink → depth gauge → tap → screwdriver**

### Drill bit
- Parts → **shank** · **centre tip** (first bite) · **cutting edge** · **flutes** (carry debris) (Nagah)
- Two flutes = standard · **three flutes** → oblique drilling, less skidding (Nagah)
- **Sharp bit → no light reflection at the tip** · blunt → tip reflects light (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Drill bit parts (Nagah)
- Sharp versus blunt drill bit tips (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Heat necrosis
- About **two-thirds** of drilling energy cuts bone · rest → heat, vibration, sound (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Heat → osteocyte death in a **cone around the bit** → screw loosening, dead bone harbours infection (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Bone cells die above **50°C** · self-drilling pins can exceed 55°C (Rockwood)
- Wires >**2 mm** without predrilling → thermal necrosis, ring sequestrum (Rockwood)

| Increases heat necrosis | Decreases heat necrosis |
|---|---|
| dull drill bit | new sharp bit |
| long drilling time | continuous saline irrigation |
| excessive thrust or speed | staged drilling for large holes |
| wobbling bit | clean the flutes between holes (Prof Abdel Karim) |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Sharp bit · saline · staged drilling · clean flutes** → no heat necrosis

- Cone of thermal damage around a drill bit (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Drill sleeve (drill guide)
- Protects soft tissue, keeps direction, **centres the pilot hole** in the gliding hole → coaxial holes (Prof Abdel Karim) · matched sleeve for each hole (AO)

### Countersink
- Prepares a seat → head contact area ↑ → **contact stress ↓**, no microfracture under the head (AO)
- **Near cortex only**, direct bone fixation only · not through a plate · not in cancellous bone → washer (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Screw through a plate → nearly **twice the torque** of an isolated screw before failure (AO)

- Countersink tool and stress under the head (AO)
- Stress under the head, without and with countersink (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Depth gauge
- Hook fully out and engaged on the far cortex (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Hold it at the **obtuse angle** → true length · acute angle → reads **too short**, add 2–4 mm (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Screw length = **top of the head to the tip** (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Depth gauge: correct versus too-short reading (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Tap
- Cuts the female thread = **outer diameter**, same pitch (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Always through a **tap sleeve** → no toggling, no second track (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Tap cuts **on withdrawal too** → withdraw gently (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Dense bone → reverse **half a turn every 3–4 turns** forward to clear chips (AO)

- **Osteoporotic and cancellous bone** → no tap, or near cortex only → tapping lowers pull-out (AO)

- Tap through a tap sleeve (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Tap, photo (Prof Abdel Karim)
- T-handle tap, photo (Nagah)

PITFALL — how many turns before reversing the tap?
- Nagah → two turns forward, half a turn back
- AO → half a turn back for every **three or four** forward
- Say → "**reverse half a turn every few turns to clear debris; by hand, through a sleeve**"

### Screwdriver, washer, length
- Screwdriver tip must **fit the recess** → worn tip → 4.7 (AO)
- Lag and plate screws → tighten to about **2/3** of the possible torque · titanium gives less feel than steel (AO)

- 4.5 cortex screw → **≈670 N** of axial force per **1 Nm** of torque (AO)
- **Washer** → flat side on bone, countersunk side takes the head → stops sinking in thin metaphyseal cortex (Nagah)
- Ideal length → **just past the far cortex** · self-tapping → 4.2 · no structure at risk → "**better long and wobbly than short and loose**" (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Washer, photo (Nagah)

### Cannulated screw — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "cannulated screw"
- "**Hollow screw** put over a **guide wire** → position checked on fluoroscopy before drilling; usually cancellous, self-drilling self-tapping."
- "Femoral neck, malleoli, scaphoid; core enlarged to keep strength, but **less pull-out** than a solid screw of the same size."

1) Guide wire → check position on AP and lateral views (Prof Abdel Karim)
2) Measure over the wire → cannulated drill → screw over the wire (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Core enlarged for the channel → bending strength **minimally affected** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Thread depth ↓ → 4 mm cannulated screws ≈**16% less** pull-out (Rockwood)
- Wire precision ↓ in dense bone and with long thin wires (Rockwood) · neck use → ch 6
- Young femoral neck → **tap** the dense cancellous bone → the head does not rotate as the screw goes in (Rockwood)

- Cannulated screws on guide wires (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Headless compression screw (Herbert, Acutrak) — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "Herbert screw"
- "**Headless, double-pitch** screw: the leading thread has the **larger pitch**, so it advances faster than the trailing thread → fragments drawn together."
- "Buried below the surface → **scaphoid**, small articular fragments (femoral head); usually no removal."

- **Compression by pitch difference** → leading coarse pitch travels further than the trailing fine pitch (Prof Abdel Karim)
- **Acutrak** → tapered, **variable pitch** along its whole length, self-tapping (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Cannulated Herbert–Whipple and AO screws → union **100%** in both groups in a scaphoid series (Campbell)

- Herbert double-pitch screws (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Double-pitch screw compressing a fracture (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Acutrak variable-pitch screws (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Two headless screws in the scaphoid, X-ray (Gupta 2025)

### Syndesmotic (position) screw — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "syndesmotic screw"
- "A **position screw** from fibula to tibia, **no gliding hole** → holds the reduced syndesmosis without compressing it."
- "One or two **3.5 or 4.5 mm** cortex screws, **2–3 cm above the plafond**, parallel to the joint, **30° anterior**."

- Reduce the syndesmosis **open**, under direct view → fewer malreductions (Campbell)
- **Three or four cortices** · four cortices → breaks rather than loosens, both ends removable (Campbell)
- Too proximal → fibula deforms, mortise widens · not parallel → fibula shifts proximally (Campbell)
- Removal → no routine removal unless symptomatic; keep **≥12 weeks** if removing (Campbell)

- Position screw across the syndesmosis (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Fibular plate with a transfixing syndesmotic screw, X-ray (Campbell)

PITFALL — "maximum dorsiflexion" for the syndesmotic screw
- Nagah → insert in maximum dorsiflexion, so the wide anterior talus does not get trapped
- Campbell → data refute this; maximal dorsiflexion may cause **external rotation malreduction**
- Say → "**traditional teaching is dorsiflexion; what matters is an anatomical, directly seen reduction**"

### Unicortical (monocortical) screw
- Hold **inferior to bicortical** screws → few indications (AO) · resists **axial load** (Nagah)
- Uses → periprosthetic fractures · temporary reduction plates · supplement in good diaphyseal bone (AO)
- Unicortical locked screws alone → **poor rotational control** (Rockwood)
- Self-drilling monocortical locking screws → failures → advance to engage the far cortex, not beyond (AO)

- Self-drilling screw: too short versus engaging the far cortex (AO)

### Poller (blocking) screw
- **Krettek, 1999** · named after bollards → narrows a **wide metaphyseal canal** (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Forces the nail central → reduction + stability · placed on the **acute-angle side** of the fragment axis and fracture line (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Placed **perpendicular** to the direction the nail would displace (AO) · details → ch 7

- Poller screws: distal femur and proximal tibia (Prof Abdel Karim)

### Bioabsorbable screws
- Poly-alpha-hydroxy acids (alpha-polyesters) → **no MRI artefact**, no removal (Prof Abdel Karim)
- First famous use → ACL graft fixation → ch 9 (Prof Abdel Karim)

- Bioabsorbable screws (Prof Abdel Karim)

4.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does a screw fail?"
- "**Pull-out** (stripped bone thread), **breakage** at the run-out by bending or torque, **loosening** from micromotion, and **heat necrosis** from bad drilling."
- "Most are technique errors: no plan, bad position, no reduction, too much force (AO)."

| Failure | Why | Prevent |
|---|---|---|
| **Stripping** of bone thread | overtorque, osteoporosis → hold lost for ever (AO) | 2/3 torque, sharp tap |
| **Stripped recess** | worn screwdriver, high torque (AO) | check the tip |
| **Head shear** during insertion | no tap, small (<4 mm) screw in dense bone (Rockwood) | tap young cortex |
| **Breakage at run-out** | torsion, eccentric or tilted hole (Prof Abdel Karim) | centred, perpendicular hole |
| **Fatigue breakage** | small core, loose plate screws (Rockwood) | larger core, tight screws |
| **Loosening** | **micromotion** at the thread → fibrous tissue (AO) | stable construct |
| **Heat necrosis** | blunt bit, no irrigation (Prof Abdel Karim) | sharp bit, saline, sleeve |

- Loose screws → next screw overloaded → **progressive loosening**, worst in osteoporotic bone (AO)
- Too much countersinking → head sinks into the canal → no compression (Prof Abdel Karim)
- Long self-drilling tip beyond the far cortex → nerves, vessels, tendons at risk (AO)
- Self-tapping screw stuck by ingrowth → **first turn clockwise** to shear the bone, then remove (AO)

- Too much countersinking: head sinks through the cortex (Prof Abdel Karim)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Strip · snap · loosen · burn** → torque, run-out, micromotion, drill

4.08.b:
| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| What is a screw? Its parts? | rotation into linear motion · head, shank, run-out, thread, tip |
| Weakest part of a screw? | **run-out** → stress riser, breaks here |
| Pitch vs lead? | pitch = distance between adjacent threads · lead = advance per 360° turn |
| What sets the drill and the tap? | pilot = core · gliding = outer · tap = outer |
| Drill for 4.5 and 3.5 screws? | 3.2 and 2.5 · 6.5 cancellous → 3.2 drill, 6.5 tap |
| Cortex vs cancellous screw? | fine shallow thread, no shank vs deep coarse thread, smooth shank |
| Self-tapping vs non-self-tapping? | flutes reduce contact → less pull-out · blunt: tap first, higher pull-out |
| When fully threaded? | cortex screws always → plate screw, position screw, lag by technique |
| Is lag a screw type? | no → a **technique** · a 4.5 lag screw gives about 2,000–3,000 N |
| Lag by technique steps? | reduce → glide → pilot → countersink → measure → tap → screw |
| Why must a lag screw be perpendicular? | not perpendicular → shear → less compression or displacement |
| Position vs lag screw? | position: thread hole only, no glide hole → no compression · lag: glide hole |
| Syndesmotic screw in dorsiflexion? | traditional teaching · what matters = an anatomical, directly seen reduction (Campbell) |
| Unicortical screw? | resists axial load · poor rotational control |
| Locking screw as lag? | no → head locks in plate · **cannot be a lag screw** |
| Sharp or blunt drill bit? | sharp → no light reflection at the tip |
| Countersink through a plate? | no → near cortex, direct bone fixation only |
| Depth gauge reads short? | acute angle → reads too short, add 2–4 mm · hold it obtuse |
| Herbert screw principle? | headless, double pitch → **compression by pitch difference** |
| Poller screw? | narrows a wide metaphyseal canal → forces the nail central |
